analysis.one_liner: Blocks the EPA from strengthening ozone smog limits until most polluted counties meet the current ones.
analysis.headline: The bill to block EPA from tightening ozone smog standards never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate environment committee until the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the EPA from tightening the national ozone standard — the limit on smog, which worsens asthma and other lung disease — until at least 85% of counties currently violating the standard had cleaned up their air. It would also have required the EPA to count only counties with direct air monitors as violating the standard, to weigh cost and feasibility, and to produce a cost-benefit analysis that ignored health benefits from reducing pollutants other than ozone. The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main gainers would have been ozone-emitting industries — refineries, power plants, and manufacturers — which would have avoided the cost of new pollution controls that a stricter ozone standard would require. Counties would also have avoided nonattainment designations, which carry restrictions on federal highway funding and new industrial permits, and the narrower monitoring rule would have meant fewer areas officially counted as polluted.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Refineries, power plants, and heavy manufacturers

how_it_helps.text: It would have prohibited the EPA from lowering the ozone standard below its January 1, 2014 level until at least 85% of counties that were violating that standard had achieved full compliance, freezing the existing limit in place for years regardless of new health evidence.

It would have required the EPA to count only counties with direct air-quality monitors as violating the standard, rather than using modeling, which would have shortened the list of areas officially required to reduce ozone.

It would have required the EPA to weigh feasibility and cost when setting the ozone standard and to produce at least one analysis counting only ozone-related benefits, excluding benefits from reducing other pollutants that the same controls would cut.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would have fallen on people's health: stronger ozone limits, which reduce asthma attacks and other respiratory illness, would have been blocked for years. Communities near polluting facilities, children, the elderly, and people with asthma would have breathed air with more smog than under the tightened standard, and the narrowed monitoring rules could have left some polluted areas officially unmeasured and unaddressed.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with asthma and communities near polluters

drawbacks.text: The bill would have barred the EPA from strengthening the ozone standard — the limit on smog linked to asthma, reduced lung function, and premature deaths — until at least 85% of the counties already violating the current standard came into compliance, which under the bill's own logic could take many years or never happen.

It would have required the EPA to designate a county as violating the ozone limit only on the basis of direct air monitors, not modeling — but not every county has a monitor, so pollution could go unmeasured in places without equipment, shrinking the list of areas officially required to clean up.

It would have required at least one cost-benefit analysis that excluded any health benefits from reducing pollutants other than ozone — controls on ozone-forming emissions also cut soot and other harmful pollution, so excluding those benefits would make the rule look far more expensive to society than it would actually be.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have saved refineries, power plants, and manufacturers substantial compliance costs, and its sponsors' core argument — that a stricter ozone rule would put hundreds of counties into nonattainment, threatening jobs and federal highway funds, and that EPA was padding its benefit math with reductions in other pollutants — was a real and seriously made objection. But the way the bill addressed it was blunt: rather than recalibrating one rule, it would have frozen national ozone standards indefinitely regardless of what the health science showed, narrowed how polluted areas are counted, and stripped the health benefits of cleaner air out of the official analysis. On balance, the costs fell on public health and the gains went to a concentrated set of polluting industries, and the bill's death left the trade-off unresolved rather than settled on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator John Thune introduced the Clean Air, Strong Economies (CASE) Act on September 17, 2014, joined at introduction by Senator McConnell and eleven other Republican senators.

The bill targeted the EPA's ongoing review of the ground-level ozone standard — the health-based limit on smog — and would have prohibited the agency from lowering that standard until at least 85% of the counties violating it had come into compliance.

It also would have required the EPA to designate violating counties only on the basis of direct air monitors rather than modeling, to weigh cost and feasibility, and to publish a benefit analysis that ignored health gains from cutting pollutants other than ozone.
After being read twice and referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, the bill received no further action of any kind before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
All 14 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democratic senator ever supported the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people kept the existing ozone protections untouched, because the rollback the bill would have enacted never advanced far enough to become law; the industries that would have saved compliance costs gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyday people; the ozone rollback never became law.

for.name: John Thune
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to freeze the ozone standard and restrict how the EPA designates violating counties.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a purely Republican effort: all 14 cosponsors were Republicans, no Democrat backed it, and the Democratic committee chair never moved it.

industries.note: Refineries are major sources of the emissions that form ground-level ozone and face some of the largest costs under a stricter standard. The bill would have frozen the existing limit and narrowed which counties count as violating it, sparing those facilities expensive upgrades — with the cost passed to the public as smog-related illness.

Power plant emissions are a principal contributor to ozone pollution, and a tighter standard would have forced new pollution controls. The bill's freeze on standards and its cost-and-feasibility requirements would have deferred or avoided those costs.

Factories in ozone-forming regions face compliance costs and the possibility of nonattainment designations, which can trigger restrictions on federal highway funding and new permitting burdens. The bill would have eased both the standard and the designation process.

industries.industry: State and local governments in ozone counties
industries.note: The bill would have spared counties the regulatory burden of a nonattainment designation, which can restrict highway funds. But their residents would have breathed dirtier air for longer, and the narrower monitoring requirement could have left local pollution officially unmeasured.
